subject: maths
pattern: Integrals carries 12-14 marks in the Karnataka 2nd PUC maths paper, the highest-weight maths chapter: 1-mark standard integrals and definite integral values, 2-mark direct, substitution and by-parts integrals, 3-mark partial fractions, completing the square, e^x[f+f'] and property-based definite integrals, and a 5-mark question on the standard formula or a King-property definite integral. Examiners expect the substitution or method to be named, the constant of integration C for indefinite integrals, and limits applied correctly for definite integrals.

questions.answer: Integrate by parts with $u=x$, $dv=e^xdx$: $\displaystyle\int xe^xdx=xe^x-\int e^xdx=xe^x-e^x+C=e^x(x-1)+C$.
Let $f(x)=\sin^3x$. $f(-x)=-\sin^3x=-f(x)$, so $f$ is an odd function. For an odd function $\displaystyle\int_{-a}^{a}f(x)dx=0$. Hence the value is $0$.

Write $\dfrac{1}{(x-1)(x-2)}=\dfrac{A}{x-1}+\dfrac{B}{x-2}$. Then $1=A(x-2)+B(x-1)$. Put $x=1$: $A=-1$. Put $x=2$: $B=1$. So the integral $=\displaystyle\int\left(\dfrac{1}{x-2}-\dfrac{1}{x-1}\right)dx=\log|x-2|-\log|x-1|+C=\log\left|\dfrac{x-2}{x-1}\right|+C$.

$\dfrac{1+\sin x}{1+\cos x}=\dfrac{1+2\sin\frac x2\cos\frac x2}{2\cos^2\frac x2}=\dfrac12\sec^2\dfrac x2+\tan\dfrac x2$. Let $f(x)=\tan\dfrac x2$, then $f'(x)=\dfrac12\sec^2\dfrac x2$. So the integral is $\int e^x[f(x)+f'(x)]dx=e^xf(x)+C=e^x\tan\dfrac x2+C$.

Let $I=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\dfrac{\sin x}{\sin x+\cos x}dx$. Using $\int_0^af(x)dx=\int_0^af(a-x)dx$: $I=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\dfrac{\cos x}{\cos x+\sin x}dx$. Adding: $2I=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}1\,dx=\dfrac\pi2$. Hence $I=\dfrac\pi4$.

Write as $\int1\cdot\sin^{-1}x\,dx$ and integrate by parts: $=x\sin^{-1}x-\displaystyle\int\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}dx$. Put $t=1-x^2$, $dt=-2x\,dx$: $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{x\,dx}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}=-\sqrt{1-x^2}$. Hence $\displaystyle\int\sin^{-1}x\,dx=x\sin^{-1}x+\sqrt{1-x^2}+C$.
Put $t=1+x^2$, so $dt=2x\,dx$. When $x=0$, $t=1$; when $x=1$, $t=2$. The integral $=\dfrac12\displaystyle\int_1^2\dfrac{dt}{t}=\dfrac12[\log t]_1^2=\dfrac12\log2$.

Let $I=\int\sqrt{a^2-x^2}\,dx=x\sqrt{a^2-x^2}-\int x\cdot\dfrac{-x}{\sqrt{a^2-x^2}}dx$ (by parts, taking $1$ as second function) $=x\sqrt{a^2-x^2}-\int\dfrac{(a^2-x^2)-a^2}{\sqrt{a^2-x^2}}dx=x\sqrt{a^2-x^2}-I+a^2\sin^{-1}\dfrac xa$. So $2I=x\sqrt{a^2-x^2}+a^2\sin^{-1}\dfrac xa$. Hence $I=\dfrac x2\sqrt{a^2-x^2}+\dfrac{a^2}2\sin^{-1}\dfrac xa+C$.

Let $I=\displaystyle\int_0^\pi\dfrac{x\sin x}{1+\cos^2x}dx$. Using $\int_0^af(x)dx=\int_0^af(a-x)dx$: $I=\displaystyle\int_0^\pi\dfrac{(\pi-x)\sin x}{1+\cos^2x}dx$. Adding: $2I=\pi\displaystyle\int_0^\pi\dfrac{\sin x}{1+\cos^2x}dx$. Put $t=\cos x$, $dt=-\sin x\,dx$; limits $1$ to $-1$: $2I=\pi\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1}\dfrac{dt}{1+t^2}=\pi[\tan^{-1}t]_{-1}^{1}=\pi\left(\dfrac\pi4+\dfrac\pi4\right)=\dfrac{\pi^2}2$. Hence $I=\dfrac{\pi^2}4$.
